scenarios.name: floor
scenarios.title: the product's legibility floor (720p)
scenarios.why: the lowest rung the floor allows is twice the link's capacity, so the picture cannot be made small enough to fit: the ladder must hold the floor and let the bitrate be throttled instead

invariants.detail: the link dropped packets, so it was genuinely at capacity
the receiver kept receiving data throughout the saturation phase
the ladder stepped down when the link saturated
the estimator never raised its target on a report that said the link was congested (the AIMD regression guard)
the ladder converged onto the link's capacity instead of overshooting it
the offered load converged onto the link's capacity
the ladder climbed back once the link freed up
the stream carried more data after the recovery than during the saturation
the ladder moved a bounded number of times

scenarios.name: unfloored
scenarios.title: no resolution floor
scenarios.why: the ladder may descend to a rung that does fit, so the offered load converges onto the link's capacity

notes: The bandwidth estimator, the token-bucket pacer and the resolution ladder are the in-tree implementations — the same ones the engine drives. The datagrams travel over a real UDP socket pair.

The congestion is real: the receiving side enforces a token-bucket capacity and drops the datagrams that arrive when the bucket is empty, exactly as a bottleneck router's queue overflows. The loss the estimator reacts to is therefore a real loss of real packets.

What is modelled is the link itself (a fixed-capacity, loss-on-overflow bottleneck) and the peer (a receiver that reports loss, RTT and optionally REMB once per reporting interval). There is no ICE, DTLS, SRTP or codec in the path: the benchmark measures the rate-control closed loop, not the transport stack.

The 'floor' scenario is the product's case: the resolution floor makes the lowest allowed rung twice the link's capacity, so the ladder holds the floor and the bitrate is throttled instead. The 'unfloored' scenario lets the ladder descend to a rung that fits.

The numbers are machine-dependent (the loopback's real RTT and the host's real scheduling jitter), so the committed artifact is one local sample, not a pass/fail threshold. What must hold on every machine are the invariants, and they are asserted by tools/benchmark_saturation.py and recorded in the artifact.

The regression guard for an AIMD defect this benchmark uncovered: the estimator used to resume its additive increase once the cooldown expired even while the link was still lossy, so the estimate walked back up to the rate that had just been throttled. The Goog-CC front-end already carried that guard; the AIMD one did not.

The guard is decided on the estimator's own per-report reason ('aimd_increase' / 'remb_override' on a report whose loss rate is at or above the estimator's 2% congestion threshold), not on the before/after estimate pair: the reported estimate is an exponentially smoothed value, so it can drift upwards by a few bits after a decrease without the estimator having raised anything. The artifact's 'reports' array carries the raw evidence.
